one_liner: C++20 reflection serializer that reads JSON into structs through embedded yyjson; claims ~2x hand-written RapidJSON, ~10x nlohmann/json.
what_it_does: Maps plain aggregate structs to and from JSON without per-type boilerplate: rfl::json::read<T>(str) returns rfl::Result<T>, and rfl::json::write(obj) returns a std::string. Field names come from the member identifiers at compile time. Wrappers such as rfl::Rename, rfl::Validator, rfl::TaggedUnion and rfl::Flatten, plus processors such as SnakeCaseToCamelCase, NoExtraFields and DefaultIfMissing, control the mapping, and the same struct also serializes to about 15 other formats (msgpack, flexbuffers, CBOR, BSON, YAML, TOML, Avro, Cap'n Proto, Parquet, CSV and more). It is a typed binding layer, not a DOM library, so it replaces the struct-filling code you write around RapidJSON or nlohmann/json rather than their APIs.
how_it_is_fast: The parsing is done by yyjson, which is vendored as version 0.12.0 and builds an immutable DOM. The README credits yyjson for the speed. reflect-cpp then walks that DOM once with code generated per struct. In C++20 mode, field names come from structured bindings plus parsing std::source_location::function_name() at compile time; C++26 mode uses P2996 std::meta instead. Each JSON key is compared (string_view ==) against the compile-time field names in a fold expression, and each value is placement-new'd straight into an uninitialized, aligned stack buffer of T through a view of member pointers, so no struct is default-constructed first. Writes build a yyjson mutable DOM, serialize it with yyjson_mut_write_opts and copy the result into a std::string.
when_to_use: You now hand-write RapidJSON or nlohmann/json DOM-walking code to fill typed structs and want a one-line rfl::json::read<T> that the project says runs faster (its benchmark code needs about 50-90 lines per dataset for the other libraries).

Typed configs, API payloads and records where you also want validation (rfl::Validator, rfl::Email, rfl::Timestamp), all field errors collected into one message, and generated JSON Schema (rfl::json::to_schema<T>).

One struct model that must also go out as msgpack, flexbuffers, BSON, CBOR, YAML, Avro, Cap'n Proto or Parquet. The project's cross-format benchmarks rank flexbuffers, msgpack and yas fastest, ahead of JSON.
Workloads shaped like the benchmark: float-heavy arrays such as GeoJSON (canada), nested string-heavy records (licenses), or many small objects (person), parsed from an in-memory string.
C++20 codebases on GCC 11.4+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 17.8+ whose types are plain aggregates without user-declared constructors.
when_not_to_use: Peak parse throughput: the benchmark README says reflect-cpp is slightly slower than simdjson and yyjson used directly, so if you will hand-write the binding anyway, use those instead.
Untyped or schema-less JSON, or editing JSON in place: the tool maps into structs. rfl::Generic exists, but open issue #368 reports rfl::to_generic running more than 10x slower than rfl::json::write.

Very large or streaming inputs: read() parses the whole input into a yyjson DOM before it fills the struct, the istream overload first copies the whole stream into a std::string, and YYJSON_READ_INSITU is rejected. Peak memory is roughly input plus DOM plus output.

Build-time-sensitive projects with wide structs: issue #86 reports compiles going from seconds to minutes, a need for -fconstexpr-depth=1024/2048, and a roughly 130-member struct that was 'prohibitively long' to compile. Maintainers advise putting read/write calls in their own translation unit.

Types that are not simple aggregates in C++20 mode: custom constructors are unsupported, and C arrays and inheritance need -DREFLECT_CPP_C_ARRAYS_OR_INHERITANCE (fields must still all sit in one struct). The structured-binding path handles at most 256 fields.

integration.form: static lib (shared via REFLECTCPP_BUILD_SHARED). Also packaged for vcpkg and Conan, or as a source drop of include/ plus src/reflectcpp.cpp, src/reflectcpp_json.cpp and src/yyjson.c
integration.dependencies: JSON only: none external (yyjson, CTRE and enchantum are bundled). Every other format needs its own library, e.g. msgpack-c, yaml-cpp, libbson, flatbuffers, Apache Arrow or capnproto
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with GCC 11.4+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 17.8 (19.38)+ and CMake 3.23. The optional C++26 reflection mode needs GCC 16.2+ with -freflection
integration.platforms: Linux (CI: gcc 11-14 and clang 16-18), macOS 15 on arm64 and Intel (clang) and Windows (MSVC) all run in CI. No SIMD or ISA requirement is documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented. Each read/write call builds its own yyjson document and Reader/Writer object, and the JSON paths reviewed show no shared mutable state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces the struct-mapping code you write on top of RapidJSON or nlohmann/json, but offers no API compatible with RapidJSON's Document/Writer or nlohmann::json's DOM

gotchas: Open issue #719 (2026-08-27): rfl::json::read segfaults under GCC 12 at -O2 for some structs (internal linkage, an std::optional nested aggregate, 12+ fields). read_struct type-puns an unsigned char buffer as T. Workarounds reported: -fno-strict-aliasing, rfl::DefaultIfMissing, or GCC 11/14.
Unknown JSON keys are silently ignored by default. Add the rfl::NoExtraFields processor to reject them. Missing non-optional fields are errors unless you use DefaultIfMissing.

Errors: read returns rfl::Result and does not throw, but write() throws std::runtime_error when yyjson refuses to serialize. Open issue #421 reports Windows crashes on strings that are not UTF-8 (e.g. cp1251, some std::wstring or std::filesystem::path values).
In C++20 mode, enums reflect only values in [-256, 256] by default. Widen the range with RFL_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/RFL_ENUM_RANGE_MAX or rfl::config::enum_range<E>.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against yyjson or simdjson: pick reflect-cpp when you want typed struct binding without writing the DOM walk and can accept the small overhead its own README admits. Against glaze, the other reflection-based C++ option: the published figures come from different benchmarks and cannot be compared (glaze ~2.9x RapidJSON read, reflect-cpp 'about twice'), so choose reflect-cpp for its wide non-JSON format list (Avro, Cap'n Proto, Parquet, BSON, etc.) and pydantic-style validators rather than for raw read speed.
verified_claims_summary: The project's Google Benchmark code times reads of three datasets (canada, licenses, person) into typed structs. It compares rfl::json::read (yyjson backend) with hand-written nlohmann/json, RapidJSON (default non-insitu Parse), yyjson and simdjson on-demand code (simdjson is skipped under clang), built at -O2 Release. The runs happen in GitHub Actions: ubuntu-24.04 with gcc 11-14 and clang 16-18, macOS 15 and Windows MSVC, with no CPU model given. The only published result is prose ('usually about twice as fast' as RapidJSON, 'about 10 times faster' than nlohmann/json, slightly slower than simdjson and yyjson), because per-run numbers exist only in Actions job step summaries that could not be retrieved through the API or an anonymous fetch.
status_note: Actively maintained by getML (Code17 GmbH): last commit 2026-09-22, v0.25.0 released 2026-05-16, ~1.9k stars. MIT-licensed and available through vcpkg and Conan, so it is easy to adopt, though GCC 12 users should note open issue #719.
